source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Full text read. With oracle labels telling the model when to stop, self-correction helps a lot. Without oracle labels (intrinsic), accuracy falls with more rounds.
numbers: Oracle (GPT-3.5 / GPT-4): GSM8K 75.9->95.5 / 84.3->97.5; CommonSenseQA 75.8->82.0 / 89.7->85.5; HotpotQA 26.0->49.0 / 29.0->59.0. Intrinsic GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (3 calls) -> 74.7 (5 calls); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8. GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49 -> 49 -> 43. Feedback-prompt table (GPT-4-Turbo): baselines 62.0 and 64.0 fall to 24-58 after one or two rounds.
quote: improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: Also says multi-agent debate is no better than self-consistency at an equal number of responses. Small subsets (HotpotQA 100 items).
agent_relevance: A practice-style retry loop with no external check can lower accuracy. Gate every retry on a real check and compare against resampling at equal calls.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Full text read. At equal sample budget, repair is often no better than fresh i.i.d. sampling, especially at small budgets. More initial programs help more than more repairs.
numbers: Models: CodeLlama-13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS. More initial programs (np) give consistent relative gains; more feedback-repairs (nfr) give marginal gains at higher budgets and often lower performance at lower budgets. On APPS marginal gains for GPT-3.5 only at the largest np.
quote: the most important factor ... is the diversity of the base samples that are generated up-front, rather than the diversity of the repairs
limits: Budget counted in samples/tokens; self-contained Python tasks only. Feedback quality is the bottleneck: human feedback gave higher repair success than GPT-4 feedback.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of the dose-response gap: more targeted retries plateau fast; breadth of first attempts wins at equal cost. Split budget between fresh samples and repairs.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Full text read. The only clean per-iteration curve in the self-feedback literature: gains per iteration shrink; generic feedback helps less than specific feedback; some tasks do not rise monotonically.
numbers: Headline about 20% absolute average improvement (abstract), up to 13% absolute on code. Per iteration: Code Optimization 22.0 -> 28.8 after 3 iterations; Sentiment Reversal 33.9 -> 36.8; Constrained Generation 29.0 -> 49.7. With no or generic feedback one task fell 56.4 -> 48.0 across iterations. Acronym generation not monotone.
quote: the marginal improvement naturally decreases with more iterations
limits: Compares to single-pass output, NOT to a sampling baseline at equal tokens, which Huang 2023 and Kamoi 2024 call an unfair comparison. Part of the scoring is by GPT-4 judges.
agent_relevance: Evidence for diminishing returns of practice-like iterations (cap loops near 2 to 3). Headline gains overstate the net effect once budget is matched.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Full text read. Gains depend on an executable test signal. On the hardest problems, reflection without tests hurts and without a written lesson adds nothing.
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. Ablation on the 50 hardest HumanEval-Rust problems: full Reflexion 60%; without test generation 52%; without the written self-reflection step no gain over the base run. On MBPP Python Reflexion is below GPT-4 (80% base) because of false-positive tests.
quote: the agent is unable to determine if the current implementation is correct without unit tests
limits: Success depends on test quality and premature stops from flaky tests. Not budget-matched against best-of-N.
agent_relevance: Retry practice works when the check is external and good; a weak self-made check can lock in wrong answers. Check quality is the limit, like feedback quality in deliberate practice.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Full text read. Supervised STaR-style and pair-SFT training on correction traces do not give real self-correction; the second attempt is no better or worse than the first. RL with a shaped reward gives a gain.
numbers: MATH, base model: attempt 1 52.6%, attempt 2 41.4% (delta -11.2); STaR 55.4 -> 41.2 (-14.2); STaR variant 53.6 -> 54.0 (+0.4); Pair-SFT 52.4 -> 54.2 (+1.8). Correct-to-incorrect flips 15.8% for base model, 19.6% for STaR. SCoRe: +15.6% on MATH and +9.1% on HumanEval over base self-correction (abstract).
limits: Gemini 1.5 only; gain is for trained weights, not a prompt scaffold. No independent replication seen.
agent_relevance: Even with weight training, naive practice on corrections degrades correct answers. A scaffold cannot get this by prompting; track right-to-wrong flips as the main metric.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Full text read (front matter and structure). Survey of self-correction papers by research question and whether the comparison is fair (no oracle, same budget).
numbers: Three findings: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks, except tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) self-correction works well where reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. The bottleneck is feedback generation.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey with no new experiments. 'Fair' is the authors' classification.
agent_relevance: Supports routing retry loops to tasks with reliable verifiers; supplies a checklist for a fair budget-matched test of our own loop.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Full text read. Dose-response for pure resampling: coverage rises log-linearly across orders of magnitude of samples, fitted by an exponentiated power law, when an automatic verifier exists.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, above the single-sample state of the art of the time. Tasks: GSM8K, MATH, CodeContests, MiniF2F, SWE-bench Lite.
limits: Needs a verifier; without one, majority vote and reward models plateau well before coverage. Coverage is pass@k, not what a deployed system returns.
agent_relevance: Gives the shape of a no-plateau practice curve (many verified attempts). Contrast with d01 and d02 where sequential self-repair plateaus. Test our loop against this baseline at equal tokens.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can Be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Full text read. The best test-time strategy depends on question difficulty. Routing by estimated difficulty beats a fixed best-of-N, and on the hardest bin no method makes meaningful progress.
numbers: Five difficulty bins from the base model's own pass rate. Compute-optimal allocation beats best-of-N with about 4x less test-time compute. Small model plus test-time compute vs a 14x larger model: preferable on easy and intermediate questions, not on hard ones when inference load is high. Level 5: 'no method makes much meaningful progress'.
quote: on the most difficult questions (level 5), no method makes much meaningful progress
limits: PaLM 2-S* on MATH only; difficulty is model-estimated, not human-rated.
agent_relevance: Closest direct evidence for gaps 2 and 3: routing on predicted difficulty beats a fixed loop, and extra practice-like compute does not rescue the hardest tier. Mirrors the flat elite tail in humans (analogy only).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Full text read (key sections). Forcing longer reasoning with 'Wait' raises accuracy up to a point, then flattens.
numbers: s1-32B with budget forcing: AIME24 50% to 57%; exceeds o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24 (abstract). Scaling eventually flattens at about six times more 'Wait' (Figure 4); the context window is a second limit.
limits: Trained on 1,000 selected examples; a few hard math sets; AIME24 has 30 problems so +7 points is about 2 problems.
agent_relevance: Sequential extra thinking has a plateau, as human practice curves do at the top. Set a stopping rule for added iterations.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
finding: Full text read (key sections). After RLVR training, pass@1 improves but at large k the base model matches or beats the trained model, so the set of solvable problems does not grow.
numbers: Pass@k with k up to 256 across math, code and visual reasoning benchmarks and several RL algorithms: base models get higher pass@k at large k; coverage (pass@256) decreases as RLVR proceeds.
limits: Pass@k at large k is a coverage test, not a cost-matched one; later work disputes the reading on other tasks.
agent_relevance: Practice and best-of-N amplify what the base already can do. Analogue of the human result that practice raises the median but does not extend the limit at the top.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning
finding: Full text read (key sections). Far-transfer analogue. Over 20 open reasoning-tuned models, most that gain on math do not gain elsewhere. In a controlled Qwen3-14B math-only test, RL (GRPO) transfers and SFT does not; SFT drifts and forgets.
numbers: Audit of 20+ models on math, other reasoning and non-reasoning tasks. Controlled Qwen3-14B: both gain on math; other-reasoning and non-reasoning gains only for the RL-tuned model (Figure 1: up to +58.6 and +7.5 for RL). SFT shows higher PCA shift and KL drift.
limits: Weight training, not a prompt scaffold; no human-style active control. Per-benchmark numbers read from a figure only.
agent_relevance: Transfer is not automatic and depends on how the practice is done. A scaffold has no weights; test cross-family transfer of stored lessons against a no-lesson control.

source: Campitelli and Gobet (2008) CogSci note: The role of deliberate practice in expertise: necessary but not sufficient (data of Gobet and Campitelli 2007)
finding: Full 2-page text read. Reports the Argentine chess sample behind the huge-spread result. The 2011 Current Directions paper was not retrievable.
numbers: N=104 players (weak amateurs to grandmasters); DP explained 34% of rating variance; mean DP to master 11,053 h; fastest 3,016 h, slowest 23,608 h (about 8x); some players with over 25,000 h never reached master; group practice predicted skill better than solitary; starting age predicted rating after controlling for hours. Longitudinal: after 3 years masters outrated experts without more practice; experts plateaued despite practice.
quote: Practice is a necessary, but not sufficient condition for reaching high levels of expertise.
limits: Conference note, not a full report; the 3,000 vs 30,000 h in our row is a rounded form of 3,016 vs 23,608 h (or the unverified 2011 text). Hours self-reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed. Use 3,016 to 23,608 h, not 3,000 to 30,000. Argues for adaptive stopping.

source: Gobet and Ereku (2014) Checkmate to deliberate practice: the case of Magnus Carlsen
finding: Full opinion text read. A top-ten check of the claim that skill rises monotonically with practice.
numbers: Carlsen rated 2881 in June 2014, 100.4 points above the mean of the next ten (M=2780.6), t(9)=-19.38, p<0.001. His estimated years of practice (18) were lower than the mean of the other ten (24.6), t(9)=2.83, p<0.05. Years estimated from starting age, not logged hours.
limits: Opinion piece with biography-sourced estimates; n=11; years not hours.
agent_relevance: Weak anecdotal support that the top tail is not set by dose. Not a main finding.

source: Debatin, Hopp, Vialle, Ziegler (2023) The meta-analyses of deliberate practice underestimate the effect size because they neglect individualization
finding: Full text read. Authors independent of Macnamara and of Ericsson. They argue the meta-analyses measured structured practice, not individualized practice, and test this on chess players.
numbers: N=178 chess players, Elo change. Structured practice added R2=0.024 (p=0.011) to age plus starting Elo; Spearman r_s(176)=0.19 with Elo change. Didactic educational capital alone added R2<0.01 (p=.26); the interaction raised R2 to 0.43 (adj. 0.41; R2 change .15, p=.005; beta=.37). Players at +1 SD didactic capital improved over 3 times faster per unit of structured practice than average players.
limits: Correlational; the individualization proxy is a questionnaire on teaching capital; one sample; main effect small (r_s=.19).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed. An outside group supports the definitional reading: tailoring and quality of practice moderate its payoff. For an agent this means targeted retry with feedback, not more retries.

source: Meinz, Hambrick, Leach, Boschulte (2023) Ability and Nonability Predictors of Real-World Skill Acquisition: The Case of Rubik's Cube Solving
finding: Full text via PMC read (abstract, intro, method). Trained novices with near-equal exposure: fluid intelligence still predicts skill; working memory and personality do not.
numbers: N=79 novices trained by 8 videos on a 7-step method in one session of up to 6 h. Higher Gf (not WMC) predicted efficient and accurate cube solving; no nonability variable (grit, growth mindset, need for cognition, big five) was associated with skill. Exact coefficients not extracted.
limits: Single session, narrow task, student sample. Hambrick (an author of the meta-analyses) is a co-author.
agent_relevance: Ability effect with exposure held about equal. Analogue: a stronger base model may gain more from the same scaffold (to be tested).

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020) Is the Deliberate Practice View Defensible?
finding: Full text downloaded and checked for gap 9: it is a defence by the original meta-analysts. Independent re-runs of the 88-study set were not found in OpenAlex or Europe PMC searches beyond Debatin 2021.
numbers: Ericsson rejected 87 of 88 effects; r .54 to .78 after correction, 61% reliable variance; reliability sensitivity 87.1% at .60 down to 38.7% at .90 (see a10, a11, b21).
limits: Interested party. Absence of independent reanalysis is from a few searches only.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: no neutral group found re-running the dataset; treat the debate as author-versus-author.

source: Corrigendum to Macnamara et al. 2014, Psychological Science 2018 (record 10.1177/0956797618769891, PMID 29733772)
finding: Record confirmed (published 7 May 2018) but the SAGE page returned 403 and no open copy was found. Per-moderator corrigendum values were NOT read.
numbers: Not available. Only the domain values via Hambrick 2020 (games 24, music 23, sports 20, education 5, professions 1, overall 14).
limits: Gap 4 stays open. Moderator-level numbers (practice method, performance method, predictability) remain original 2014 values.
agent_relevance: Keep the 4/12/24 predictability split labelled as original 2014.

source: Corrigendum to Burgoyne et al. (2016) Intelligence, 2018 (record 10.1016/j.intell.2018.08.004)
finding: Record confirmed but the Elsevier page returned 403, so whether the chess intelligence r=.24 changed was NOT confirmed.
agent_relevance: Cite chess intelligence as about .2 to .3, provisional.
